la:noun:urbs.html:
urbs, urbis (dat. VRBEI, Corp. Inscr. Lat. 206), f.
Sanscr. vardh-, to make strong; cf. Pers. vard-ana, city
,
a walled town, a city.
Lit.
In gen.: hi coetus sedem primum certo loco domiciliorum causā constituerunt: quam cum locis manuque sepsissent, ejusmodi conjunctionem tectorum oppidum vel urbem appellaverunt, delubris distinctam spatiisque communibus,; cf.: post ea qui fiebat orbis, urbis principium, Müll.: urbs dicitur ab orbe, quod antiquae civitates in orbem flebant, id. ap. : interea Aeneas urbem designat aratro, Serv.: veni Syracusas, quod ab eā urbe ... quae tamen urbs, etc.,: certabant urbem Romam Remoramne vocarent, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 85 Vahl.): arce et urbe sum orba, id. ap. (Trag. v. 114 ib.): urbes magnae et imperiosae,: urbs illa praeclara (Syracusae),: duabus urbibus eversis inimicissimis huic imperio,.— Rarely, and mostly poet., with the name of the city in gen.: urbs Patavi, Buthroti,; : Cassius in oppido Antiochiae cum omni exercitu,.—With adj. prop.: urbs Romana = Roma, ; ; ; .—Of other cities (rare and post-class.): Lampsacenae urbis salus,, ext. 4: in urbe Aquilejensi, Paul. v. S. : urbs urbium,a metropolis,.—
In partic., the city of Rome (like ἄστυ, of Athens): postquam Urbis appellationem, etiamsi nomen proprium non adiceretur, Romam tamen accipi sit receptum,; cf. ; : hujus urbis condendae principium profectum a Romulo,; cf. ; 1, 1, 1; 1, 37, 58: (Caesar) maturat ab urbe proficisci,: de urbe augendā quid sit promulgatum, non intellexi,: conditor urbis (Romulus),: (pater) Dextera sacras jaculatus arces Terruit urbem,: minatus urbi vincla,; called also urbs aeterna,.— Ad urbem esse, to stop at or near Rome; in publicists' lang., of returning generals, who had to remain outside of the city till the Senate decreed them the right of entrance; or of provincial magistrates who were preparing for departure to their provinces, Ascon.; 2, 2, 6, § 17; ; .—
Transf., as in Engl.
The city, for the citizens (rare; cf. civitas): invadunt urbem somno vinoque sepultam,: maesta attonitaque,: bene moratae, Auct. ap. .—
The capital city, metropolis (post-class.): si tam vicinum urbi municipium sit, ut, etc.,; Cod. Th. 14, 1, 3.—*
Trop.: urbem philosophiae, mihi crede, proditis, dum castella defenditis,i. e. the main point,.

la:adj:urbanus.gloss: of or belonging to a city; urban
senses: of or belonging to a city; urban
fond of, or devoted to cities
la:adj:urbanus.html:
urbānus, a, um, adj.
urbs
,
of or belonging to the city or town, city-, town- (opp. rusticus; cf.: urbicus, oppidanus).
Lit.
Adj.: nostri majores non sine causā praeponebant rusticos Romanos urbanis,, praef. § 1: rustica et urbana vita,: vita (opp. rustica),; cf. : urbani assidui cives, quos scurras vocant,: scurra,: leges,: tribus,: praetor,: plebes,: servitia,: exercitus,: administratio rei publicae (opp. provincialis),: res,; : motus,: luxus,: praedia, land and houses, all land covered by buildings (v. praedium), ; ; cf. : fundus,: rus,: cohortes,.—
Subst.: urbā-nus, i, m., an inhabitant of a city, a city man, citizen: urbani fiunt rustici,: omnes urbani, rustici,: sermo omnis non modo urbanorum, sed etiam rusticorum,: otiosi,: obrepere urbanis,.—
Esp., devoted to the city, fond of city life: diligere secessum, quem tu nimis urbanus es, nisi concupiscis,.—
Transf., in the city fashion, in the city style, citizenlike, both in a good and a bad sense.
In a good sense.
Polished, refined, cultivated, courteous, affable, urbane (syn.: comis, humanus): hominem non solum sapientem, verum etiam, ut nunc loquimur urbanum,; cf. ; so .—
Transf., of plants, improved, cultivated, ornamental: sunt arborum quaedam urbaniores, quas his placet nominibus distinguere. Hae mites, quae fructu atque aliqua dote umbrarumve officio humaniusjuvant, non improbe dicantur urbanae. : acanthi topiariae et urbanae herbae,.—
Of speech.
In gen., refined, polished, elegant. nice, choice: in vocibus nostrorum oratorum recinit quiddam et resonat urbanius,: genus dicendi,: os facile, explanatum, jucundum, urbanum, id est, in quo nulla neque rusticitas neque peregrinitas resonet,: distinctior et urbanior et altior Cicero,.—
In

partic., of wit, witty, humorous, facetious: urbanus homo erit, cujus multa bene dicta responsaque erunt: et qui in sermonibus, circulis, conviviis, item in contionibus, omni denique loco ridicule commodeque dicet, Domit. Mars. ap. : dictum per se urbanum,: circumfertur Marcii Philippi velut urbanissimum factum atque dictum,: qui est in isto genere urbanissimus,: Romani veteres atque urbani sales,: homines lauti et urbani,: hic tibi comis et urbanus liberque videtur,witty, clever,: urbanus coepit haberi,: in senatu dicax et urbanus et bellus,: urbanos qui illa censuerunt dicam an miseros? Dicerem urbanos, si senatum deceret urbanitas,.—

In a bad sense, bold, forward, impudent: frontis ad urbanae descendi praemia,: audacia,.—Adv.: urbānē (acc. to II. A.).
Courteously, civilly, affably, politely, urbanely: severe et graviter et prisce agere, an remisse ac leniter et urbane,: urbanius agere,: urbanissime et prudentissime adjuvit, Treb. Gallien. 14.—More freq.,
Of speech, wittily, acutely, elegantly, happily: aliquem facete et urbane ridere,: bene et urbane dicere,; ; : interrogare,: emendare,: urbanius elabi,: urbanissime respondere,.

la:verb:urgeo.gloss: to press, push, force, drive, urge (forward); to stimulate
senses: to press, push, force, drive, urge (forward); to stimulate
la:verb:urgeo.html:
urgeo (less correctly urgueo), ursi (
perf. rare; past part. not found), 2, v. a.
Gr. ϝεργ-, εἵργνυμι, to shut in; Sanscr. varg-, vargami, prevent; Germ. Merk; Engl. work
, to press, push, force, drive, impel, urge.
Lit. (mostly poet.; syn.: pello, trudo): unda impellitur undā Urgeturque eadem veniens urgetque priorem,: urgeris turbā circum te stante,: angustoque vagos pisces urgere catino,: trepidique pedem pede fervidus urget,; cf. : aut petis aut urges ruiturum, Sisyphe, saxum,i. e. roll up,: versaque in obnixos urguentur cornua vasto Cum gemitu,: tres (naves) Eurus ab alto In brevia et Syrtes urget,: miserum tenues in jecur urget acus,: equites in oppidum, Auct. B. Afr. 6, 3: (Mars) aetherias currus urgebat ad arces,.—
Transf.
To press upon (as something burdensome or compulsory).
To bear hard or close upon; press hard, beset (class.): Caesar cum septimam legionem, quae juxta constiterat, urgeri ab hoste vidisset,; 2, 25; ; cf.: hinc Pallas instat et urget Hinc contra Lausus,: urgent impavidi te Salaminius Teucer, te Sthenelus,: hac urget lupus, hac canis angit,. —
To weigh or bear down, to burden, oppress: at onus urget,; cf.: onus aut jam urgentis aut certe adventantis senectutis,: quod latus mundi nebulae malusque Juppiter urget,: quem scabies aut morbus urget,; cf.: ergo Quintilium perpetuus sopor Urget,: omnes illacrimabiles Urgentur ignotique longa Nocte,: populus militiā atque inopiā urguebatur,: praesens atque urgens malum,.—
To urge, press, stimulate, drive, solicit (syn. insto): quod te urget, scelus, Qui huic sis molestus?: etiam atque etiam insto atque urgeo,: quamobrem, ut facis, urge, insta, perfice,: Lepidus ursit me et suis et Antonii litteris, ut, etc., Asin. ap. : nihil urget,is pressing,: cur patrem non urserit ad exsolutionem,.—
To press, strain, exert in excess, etc.: vox autem ultra vires urgenda non est,; cf. orationem,.—
To press upon (by too great nearness), to crowd, hem in, confine: ne urbem hanc urbe aliā premere atque urgere possitis,: vallis, quam densis frondibus atrum Urget utrimque latus,; : quāque pharetratae vicinia Persidis urget,.—
Trop.
To press, ply, urge with argument (a favorite expression of Cic.): urgerent praeterea philosophorum greges ... instaret Academia,: illum neque ursi, neque levavi,: sed urges me meis versibus,: urguebat Arcesilas Zenonem, cum ipse falsa omnia diceret, etc.,.—With acc. and inf.: sed urguetis identidem hominum esse istam culpam non deorum,: illud urgeam, non intellegere eum, quid, etc.,.—Absol.: ut interrogando urgeat,: urgent tamen et nihil remittunt,; ; (also ap. ).—
To follow up, keep to, stick to, ply hard, push forward, urge on any thing: eundem locum diutius,: quin tu urges istam occasionem et facultatem,: jus, aequitatem,: idem illud de provinciis, Cael. ap. : propositum,: et durum terrae rusticus urget opus,; ; cf.: non tacta ligonibus arva,: vestem,: iter,: vestigia ad manes,: Romae cum sum et urgeo forum,am often in the Forum,; cf. altum, to force or plunge into, .— Urgeri, with gen., to be hard pressed, prosecuted for any thing: male administratae provinciae aliorumque criminum,.—Poet., with inf.: marisque Baiis obstrepentis urges Summovere litora,.—Hence, urgens, entis, P. a. (acc. to I.B.1.), pressing, cogent, urgent (postclass. and very rare): urgentior causa,: urgentissima ratio,.—Adv.: urgenter, pressingly (late Lat.), .

la:verb:urgueo.gloss: to press, push, force, drive, urge (forward); to stimulate

senses: especially of the emotions: to inflame with passion, love or lust; burn, set afire or on fire, excite, worry, disturb
to annoy, to gall, to vex
la:verb:uro.html:
ūro, ussi, ustum, 3, v. a.
for uso from root us; cf. Gr. εὔω, to singe; αὔω, to kindle
,
to burn (class.).
Lit.
In gen.: (sacer ignis) urit corpore serpens Quamcumque arripuit partem,: urere ne possit calor amplius aridus artus,: calidum hoc est: etsi procul abest, urit male,: urit odoratam nocturna in lumina cedrum,: homines in usum nocturni luminis,: picem et ceras alimentaque cetera flammae,.—
In partic.
To burn up, destroy by fire, consume (syn. cremo): hominem mortuum, inquit lex in XII., in urbe ne sepelito neve urito, Mos.; so XII. Tab. : flamma cum corpora fulva leonum soleat torrere atque urere, (902): in corpore si quid ejusmodi est, quod reliquo corpori noceat, id uri secarique patimur, : agros,: urbes hostium,: superbas Carthaginis arces,: Achaïcus Ignis Iliacas domos,; cf.: usto ab Ilio,: ustis navibus,: neglectis urenda filix innascitur agris,: cum frondibus uritur arbos, et saep.: acanthi radices ustis laxatisque mire prosunt,burned, scorched,: a sole usti,: ecce sexus infirmus se uri perpetitur,: urbis hostium,: praedas,: regionem,; .—
Of encaustic painting, to burn in (very rare): picta coloribus ustis puppis,: tabulam coloribus,.—
Transf.
To burn, i. e. to scorch, parch, dry up; to sting or pain acutely (syn. torreo): videmus ceteras partes incultas (terrarum), quod aut frigore rigeant aut urantur calore,: cum Sol gravis ureret arva,: terras (Sol),: campum (seges),: solum (cicer),: vineas (fimum suillum),: urentes harenae,; v. Orell. ad h. l.: sitis usserat herbas,: sitis arida guttur Urit,: fauces urit sitis,: nec febribus uror anhelis,: pestilentia urens simul urbem atque agros,: dysenteria si urat,: calx urit, discutit, extrahit, burns, heats (when taken as a medicine), : uri, vinciri, ferroque necari,: hae sunt, quarum Delicias et panniculus bombycinus urit,oppresses,.—
To rub sore; to gall, fret, chafe, corrode: calceus ... si pede minor, uret,: si te gravis uret sarcina chartae,: teneros urit lorica lacertos,uri virgis,: loris non ureris,: antiqua terebra urit eam partem quam perforat: Gallica excavat nec urit,: ut prensos urant juga prima juvencos,. —
To pinch with cold; to nip, blast, wither: pernoctant venatores in nive, in montibus uri se patiuntur,: Scythae continuis frigoribus uruntur,: iis, quae frigus usserit, sunt remedio,; ; : urebant montana nives,; .—
Trop., to burn, inflame, consume with passion; in pass., to burn, glow, be heated, be inflamed, be enamored; of love or lust: me tamen urit amor,: Daphnis me malus urit,: vires urit videndo Femina,: urit me Glycerae nitor, Urit grata protervitas,— Pass.: uritur infelix Dido,: ; ; ; ; 13, 763 al.: meum jecur urere bilis,: ira communiter urit utrumque,.—Pass.: uror, seu, etc.,.—Of envy: urit fulgore suo,.—
Transf.
To vex, annoy: uro hominem,I gall the fellow,; cf. pass.: id nunc his cerebrum uritur, Me esse hos trecentos Philippos facturum lucri,. —
In gen., to disturb, harass, annoy, oppress: eos bellum Romanum urebat,; cf. pass.: quo (bello) Italia urebatur,: labor aliquem urens,: captos legibus ure tuis,: populum gravis urebat infesto mari annona,: urebat nobilem populum ablatum mare,.

la:noun:urna.html:
urna, ae, f.
prop. a vessel of burnt clay; root uro
,
a vessel for drawing water, a water-pot, water-jar, urn.
Lit.: urnae dictae, quod urinant in aquā hauriendā ut urinator, Müll.; ; ; 4 (5), 11, 28; ; ; ; ; ; .—As an attribute of personified rivers, ; .—Of the constellation Aquarius, ; .—
Transf., in gen., an urn used for any purpose.
Most freq., a vessel into which were thrown the voting-tablets or lots of any kind.
A voting-urn (syn. sitella): senatorum urna copiose absolvit, equitum adaequavit,; ; ; ; ; : educit ex urnā tres (judices),; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
The urn of fate, from which is drawn the lot of every one's destiny: omnium Versatur urna serius ocius Sors exitura,: omne capax movet urna nomen,; ; : nomina in urnam coicere,; .—
A vessel to hold the ashes of the dead, a cinerary urn, ; ; ; ; 14, 441; ; ; ; .—
A money-pot, money-jar: argenti,.—
A liquid measure containing half an amphora, an urn, ; ; ; .—
A measure in gen., ; ; .

la:noun:urbanitas.gloss: An instance of living in the city; city life.
senses: An instance of living in the city; city life.
City fashions or manners; refinement, politeness, courtesy, urbanity, sophistication.
Delicacy, elegance or refinement of speech; wit, humor, pleasantry, raillery; trickery, knavery.
la:noun:urbanitas.html:
urbānĭtas, ātis, f.
id.
,
a living in a city, city life.
Lit.: desideria urbis et urbanitatis,: in urbis urbanitatisque desiderio,.—
Transf., city fashion, city manners, both in a good and in a bad sense.
In a good sense.
Refinement, elegance of manner, politeness, courtesy, affability, urbanity: addo urbanitatem, quae est virtus, ut Stoici rectissime putant,.—
Refinement, delicacy, or elegance of speech: urbanitate quādam quasi colorata oratio,; cf. (opp. rusticitas); 6, 3, 103 sq.—
In partic., wit, humor, pleasantry, raillery: contumelia si petulantius jactatur, convicium; si facetius, urbanitas nominatur,: in quantam hominum facetorum urbanitatem incurratis, non dico,: ut aliquando subtilitatem veteris urbanitatis et humanissimi sermonis attingerem,: vides exaruisse jam veterem urbanitatem,: mancipiorum urbanitas in dominos contumeliosa,: in jocis,: oratoria,: risus si aptus est, urbanitatis nomen adsequitur,; .—
In a bad sense, trickery, roguery, knavery: incuriosos milites (vernaculā utebantur urbanitate) quidam spoliavere,; so, vernula,.
